Sick-room note, Tuesday — Deepika Ma'am, school nurse
Trisha (Class 10) came in at lunch saying she felt sick. She had not eaten anything yet. A friend had told her the canteen rajma "makes everyone throw up" and that three children were ill last week. She was pale, breathing fast, one hand on her stomach, and said it started "turning" as soon as she smelled the food. No fever. I checked the canteen log: no illness reported this term. I told her so, sat with her, and we did slow breathing together. After a while she asked for her tiffin. I explained that worry can create real feelings in the stomach, what we call the nocebo effect, and asked her to tell her parents and see their doctor if the sickness keeps coming back.

qa.q: What did the canteen log show?
qa.a: No illness reported this term.

qa.q: Why did Trisha feel her stomach "turning" before eating anything?
qa.a: She expected the rajma to make her sick after what her friend said, and that anxious expectation created real queasy feelings before any food.

qa.q: Which step by Deepika Ma'am helped most, and why?
qa.a: Checking the canteen log and sharing the facts while sitting with Trisha and breathing slowly. It calmed the fear causing the nausea, and she still advised a doctor if it kept happening.

qa.q: What would change if the nurse had just told Trisha it was all in her head?
qa.a: Trisha might feel dismissed and embarrassed, stay scared of the canteen, and be less likely to report real symptoms in future.

grounding: A school nurse notes a teenager who felt nauseous before eating because she had been told the canteen food makes people sick.

passage:
Wednesday
Physio again. Good news: the ankle bends further. I've been telling myself "it's healing, it's healing" every morning, and honestly it makes the exercises easier. Varun keeps saying, "Just think positive, Pema, pain is mostly in the mind." Some of it, maybe. But the swelling in the evening is still there, and that's not my mind. So today I didn't just smile and say fine. I told the physio about the swelling and that I'd been worried it was something more. I asked her what's normal and what isn't. She took it seriously, pressed around the bone and said she'll ask the doctor to look again. I left feeling hopeful AND looked after. Both. Varun can think positive for himself.
Pema

qa.q: What was still there in the evenings?
qa.a: The swelling was still there.

qa.q: How did Pema feel leaving the physio, and why?
qa.a: Pema felt hopeful and looked after, because the positive thoughts made the exercises easier and the physio took the swelling seriously instead of brushing it off. 🙂

qa.q: What turning point did Pema choose at today's session?
qa.a: Instead of smiling and saying "fine", Pema told the physio about the swelling and the worry and asked what's normal, so hope didn't replace proper care.

qa.q: Why might Varun say "pain is mostly in the mind"?

grounding: A young adult keeps a hopeful outlook during recovery but still reports a lasting symptom and asks for balanced information instead of dismissing it.

passage:
Observation note, KG-B — Mehak Ma'am
Sonali, 5, rarely spoke in circle time. Last Tuesday she named every shape on the chart, and I said, "What a bright girl!"
Since then I've noticed I smile at her first, wait longer for her answers and hand her the harder puzzles. And Sonali has changed. She raises her hand, tries the tricky puzzles and told a friend, "I'm good at shapes, I can help you." Yesterday she stayed with a big puzzle all period.
Did she change, or did my attention change her? Next week I'll give every quiet child the same waiting time and smiles.

qa.q: What did Sonali name last Tuesday?
qa.a: Every shape on the chart.

qa.q: What does Sonali saying "I'm good at shapes, I can help you" suggest about how she sees herself?
qa.a: She now sees herself as capable, because the teacher's smiles, patient waiting and harder puzzles told her she is bright. 😊

qa.q: What does Mehak Ma'am plan next, and why is it fair?
qa.a: She will give every quiet child the same waiting time and smiles, so all of them get the chance to feel capable, not only Sonali.

qa.q: What might it be like for the other quiet children in KG-B while Sonali gets extra smiles?
qa.a: They get less waiting time and fewer hard puzzles, so trying may feel less worthwhile for them, even though nobody means it.

grounding: A teacher notices that after calling a child bright she gave her more time, smiles and challenge, and the child began to act bright.

passage: At the anganwadi in the village near Dharwad, Lokesh Sir held up a picture of a cow. "Who knows how many legs?" Shankar, five, shouted, "Four!" "Shabaash! Our clever Shankar," Sir beamed. After that, Sir always looked at Shankar first. He sat him in front, let him hand out the slates and waited with a smile when Shankar got stuck. Shankar started counting everything: goats on the path, rotis at dinner, stars from the roof. At home he told his Ajji, "I am clever. Sir said." Then he counted her bangles, twice, just to be sure.

qa.q: What did Shankar start counting?
qa.a: Goats on the path, rotis at dinner, stars from the roof, and Ajji's bangles.

qa.q: Why did Shankar tell Ajji "I am clever. Sir said."?
qa.a: Being called clever and treated that way made him believe it, and he felt proud enough to show it by counting everything.

qa.q: How could Lokesh Sir use what happened with Shankar to help the other children?
qa.a: He could give every child turns in front, jobs like the slates and the same patient smile, since being treated as capable made trying worthwhile for Shankar.

qa.q: How might a child who always sits at the back feel watching Shankar hand out the slates every day?
qa.a: That child might feel less noticed and less keen to try, since the warm attention seems saved for "the clever one".

grounding: A small boy who is called clever gets more attention and patience from his teacher and starts acting clever, counting everything around him.

passage: In the kindergarten in Bergen, Ingrid bent down to Astrid's drawing of a snail. "You noticed the spiral on its shell! You're our little scientist." The next morning, Astrid arrived with muddy boots, holding a jar. "I found a worm for science." Ingrid laughed, crouched beside her and asked what worms eat. Astrid thought hard. "Leaves? I will check." All week, Ingrid saved her a seat by the window and asked, "What does our scientist think?" Astrid began asking her own questions. Why is the rain cold? Where do snails sleep? She asked them loudly, as if they mattered.

qa.q: What did Astrid bring in the jar?
qa.a: A worm, "for science".

qa.q: Why did Astrid start asking her questions so loudly?
qa.a: Being called "our little scientist" made her feel her ideas mattered, so asking felt worthwhile and she wanted to be heard.

qa.q: How could Ingrid make sure other children get the same boost?
qa.a: Ingrid could notice something specific in each child's work and offer the same window seat and "what do you think?", so every child feels capable.

qa.q: What would change if Ingrid had walked past the snail drawing?
qa.a: Astrid might never have brought the worm or asked about rain and snails; without being treated as capable, trying might not have felt worth it.

grounding: A young child called a little scientist by her teacher receives warm attention and begins to behave like one, asking questions eagerly.

subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]
passage: In the one-room school outside Bhilwara, Usha Ma'am once said, "Vishal is weak at maths, let him copy from the board." She didn't say it again. She didn't need to. When she asked questions, her eyes moved past Vishal to the front row. If he started to answer, she waited only a moment before turning to someone else. Nobody asked him to come to the board anymore. By winter, Vishal kept his hand in his lap even when he knew the answer. He counted his father's goat money correctly every evening at home, but at school he left the sums blank. "I am weak," he told his little sister when she asked for help.

qa.q: What did Vishal count correctly every evening at home?
qa.a: His father's goat money.

qa.q: Why did Vishal keep his hand in his lap even when he knew the answer?
qa.a: After being called weak and passed over again and again, he came to believe he was bad at maths, so trying seemed pointless.

qa.q: What could Usha Ma'am change in how she asks questions?
qa.a: She could wait as long for Vishal as for the front row and invite him to the board again, showing she expects him to be able to answer.

qa.q: How might Vishal's little sister be affected when he says "I am weak"?
qa.a: She loses a helper, and she may learn from her brother that a label means you stop trying. 😔

grounding: A village boy labelled weak at maths gets less waiting time and fewer questions, stops raising his hand and begins to live down to the label.

subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]
passage: In Abebe's school in Toronto, the maths groups had animal names, but everyone knew the Turtles were the slow ones. Abebe had been a Turtle since he arrived from Addis Ababa. Ms. Yara was kind, but when she asked a hard question, she looked at the Eagles table. When Abebe raised his hand, she'd say, "Let's give someone else a turn," and move on quickly. By spring, he had stopped raising it. On a quiz he froze at a fractions question he had done at home with his uncle, and wrote nothing. "Turtles don't do fractions," he mumbled to his friend. At home that night, he solved the same question in two minutes.

qa.q: Which table did Ms. Yara look at when she asked a hard question?
qa.a: The Eagles table.

qa.q: What does Abebe mumbling "Turtles don't do fractions" show about what he now believes?
qa.a: He has taken the group label as the truth about himself, so he freezes at school even though he can solve fractions at home.

qa.q: What small change could Ms. Yara make that might break this pattern?
qa.a: She could ask the Turtles hard questions too and wait for their answers, showing Abebe she expects him to handle them.

qa.q: What might Abebe's uncle think if he saw the blank quiz?
qa.a: His uncle, who worked through fractions with him at home, might be puzzled and sad, knowing Abebe can do them, and wonder what is happening at school.

grounding: A boy placed in the slow maths group gets fewer chances to answer, stops trying and freezes on work he can actually do.

subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]
passage: At the evening tuition centre, Deepak Sir divided the room without saying so. The front benches got the tricky word problems and long, patient explanations. subtype: Family verdict about who they will become [Receiver]
passage: The results came out during a wedding, of all places, in a hot, noisy hall full of relatives. Mohit got 71 percent. His cousin got 94. Before Mohit could even eat, Bade Papa announced, "Our Mohit will never be like his cousin," and a few uncles nodded. It wasn't the first time. Mohit had heard it since he was eight, and lately he had started saying it first: "I'm the average one." He slipped out to the parking area. His mother, Sudha, found him there, her sari pinned up, holding two plates. "Seventy-one, without tuition, and with your leg in plaster for a month," she said. "I watched how hard you worked. That's who you are." Mohit stared at the plate. Then, slowly, he took it.

qa.q: What percentage did Mohit get?
qa.a: 71 percent.

qa.q: Why had Mohit started calling himself "the average one"?
qa.a: He had heard since he was eight that he would never be like his cousin, and the repeated verdict slowly became how he saw himself.

qa.q: What did Sudha choose to point out in the parking area, and why might it help?
qa.a: She named his real effort, no tuition and a leg in plaster, and said that is who he is, giving him a different, hopeful story about himself. 🤍

qa.q: How might the relatives' words feel to Mohit's cousin?
qa.a: The cousin is being used as a measuring stick, which might bring pride but also pressure, and could make it awkward to be close to Mohit.

grounding: A teenager who keeps hearing he will never be like his cousin has started to believe it, while his mother's steady belief in his effort offers another view.

subtype: Family verdict about who they will become [Receiver]
passage: In the Pune flat, the cousin's photo with the district chess trophy stood on Dadi's shelf. "Dhruv, you'll never be like Neel," Dadi said most Sundays, not unkindly, as if reading out the weather. Dhruv had stopped playing chess at thirteen. At sixteen, when a teacher suggested the school team, he said, "Not my thing. Neel's the smart one." That evening his father, Manoj, set up the old board on the dining table. "One game. I'm rusty." Dhruv won in twenty moves. Manoj didn't mention Neel. He only said, "You saw that knight fork three moves ahead. That's practice, not magic. You could do more of that if you wanted." Dhruv put the pieces back slowly, looking at the knight.

qa.q: Where did Manoj set up the old chess board?
qa.a: On the dining table.

qa.q: What does Dhruv saying "Neel's the smart one" suggest about how he sees himself?
qa.a: After years of hearing he'd never be like Neel, he has come to see himself as the less smart one and turns down chances before trying.

qa.q: What choice did Manoj make that could lift Dhruv?
qa.a: Instead of comparing, he played a game, praised one specific move and said it came from practice, showing steady belief that Dhruv could grow.

qa.q: Why might Dadi say it "as if reading out the weather"?
qa.a: To Dadi it may feel like a harmless remark rather than a verdict; she may not realise how much the repeated words have shaped what Dhruv thinks he can do.

grounding: A teenager who keeps hearing he will never match his cousin gives up chess, while his father's quiet belief in practice offers a way back.
